BEVAE-181.text:
Environment = air, water, land + living beings and how they interact.
Abiotic parts (air, water, soil, light) + biotic parts (plants, animals, microbes) make one system.
The environment gives food, water, air and shelter — and takes back waste.
Human activity changes it faster than nature can repair it.
Exam point: define environment first, then give one abiotic and one biotic example.

Ecosystem = living (biotic) + non-living (abiotic) parts working together.
Producers (green plants) make food by photosynthesis.
Consumers depend on producers directly or indirectly.
Decomposers (bacteria, fungi) break down dead matter and recycle nutrients.
Energy flows one way through an ecosystem; nutrients cycle. A food web is many linked food chains in one habitat.

BEVAE-181.topic: Block 2: Natural Resources — Land, Water and Forests
BEVAE-181.text:
Natural resources are renewable (sun, wind, water, forests — if used within limits) or non-renewable (coal, oil, minerals).
Land degradation comes from deforestation, overgrazing and careless mining.
Water is scarce even though oceans are vast — most water is salty, and groundwater is being used faster than it refills.
Forests give timber, medicine, rainfall and homes to wildlife — losing them loses all four at once.

Biodiversity = variety of life: genetic, species and ecosystem diversity.
Its services are practical, not abstract: pollination, clean water, fertile soil, climate control, food and medicine.
India is a mega-diverse country — that is why its loss here matters globally.
Exam point: always name the level (genetic / species / ecosystem) when you define biodiversity.

Renewable energy (solar, wind, hydro, biomass) is renewed by nature; fossil fuels (coal, petroleum, gas) are finite.
Solar energy is the cleanest large-scale option for India — abundant sunlight, no fuel cost, no smoke.
Saving energy is also a resource: efficient bulbs, public transport and insulation cut demand without cutting comfort.
Exam point: pair each source with renewable or non-renewable, never leave it unlabelled.

Main threats: habitat loss, over-exploitation, pollution and invasive species.
In-situ conservation protects species where they live — national parks, wildlife sanctuaries, biosphere reserves.
Ex-situ conservation protects them outside — zoos, botanical gardens, seed banks.
Chipko (1973) was a forest-conservation movement: villagers hugged trees to stop them being cut.
Exam point: in-situ vs ex-situ is a standard comparison question — learn one example of each.

BEVAE-181.topic: Block 3: Pollution, Waste and Global Issues
BEVAE-181.text:
Air pollution: smoke, vehicle exhaust, dust — harms lungs and crops.
Water pollution: sewage, industrial waste, fertilisers — harms drinking water and aquatic life.
Soil pollution: pesticides and plastic waste — harms fertility.
Waste management order: reduce, reuse, recycle — then compost, then safe disposal. Landfill is the last option, not the first.
Global issues: global warming (CO2 traps heat), ozone depletion and climate change — all cross borders, so no country solves them alone.

BEVAE-181.topic: Block 4: Protecting Our Environment — Law and Ethics
BEVAE-181.text:
Key Indian laws: Environment (Protection) Act 1986; Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972; Forest (Conservation) Act 1980; National Green Tribunal Act 2010.
Sustainable development = meeting today's needs without harming future generations' ability to meet theirs.
Environmental ethics: humans are part of nature, not above it — present use must leave enough for the future.
Exam point: name the Act + year, then one thing it protects.
